GSK shares tips for keeping mature brands fresh
sum: At a recent industry conference, Andrea Luker, vaccine marketing operations and compliance, congress and peer-to-peer lead at GSK, offered the audience a candid look into a persistent challenge in pharma marketing: how to keep speaker programs for mature brands fresh, credible, and compliant long after the initial excitement has faded.

Luker explained that mature brands face a unique set of pressures that newer products do not. “A mature brand doesn’t go away. There’s still a medical need for it. That’s why it’s still on the market. So it is up to us to continue to educate,” she said. Unlike a brand launch, where novelty carries momentum, mature products must justify their continued presence in speaker programs through evidence rather than enthusiasm.

That evidence doesn’t have to be just clinical. True differentiation, noted Luker, comes from context: new patient populations, emerging evidence, shifting practice barriers, misinformation or misunderstandings, and market disruptions that create a genuine, documentable educational gap.

This is where Luker’s “relevant, differentiated, and defensible” framework comes in, built around three foundational questions she said every team must ask before advancing a program. “Is it a unique educational question? Is there an educational need? And do we have documentation?”

Luker stressed that defensibility must be engineered from the very start of program design, not retrofitted after the fact. “Compliance starts at the design stage,” she said, pointing to elements like documented educational need, clear audience definitions, explicit learning objectives, and evidence mapping as the building blocks of a program that can withstand scrutiny.

The message is that there is always an educational need that is defensible and can be compliant in mature brand programs. Luker said, you just can’t rest on cosmetic updates. “It’s not just the surface ... It’s not that we just updated the title or our visuals, our brand colors have updated it. That’s not distinct,” she told attendees.

What's Behind GSK (LSE:GSK) Shares Slipping Despite Beating Quarterly Forecasts?
sum: - GSK's quarterly sales and core operating profit came in above market expectations, led by HIV and respiratory specialty medicines.
- Vaccine sales softened as Shingrix faced destocking in China and inventory effects in the United States, while meningitis products grew.
- Shares fell as investors focused on restructuring costs, currency drag and higher interest expense, leaving the FTSE 100 drugmaker near the lower end of its recent range.

GSK (LSE:GSK) Healthcare GSK plc (LSE:GSK) 1923.50 GBX +8.500 0.444% Last Updated at: 2026-10-27T16:36:00Z is trading near the bottom of its recent range this week after a quarterly update that, on the face of it, had plenty to like. Sales rose at constant exchange rates, gross margin widened on a better product mix and manufacturing efficiencies, and both revenue and adjusted earnings came in ahead of consensus forecasts. It is a notable update for market participants who follow Healthcare Stocks listed in London.

Yet the shares fell in early dealings on results day and have struggled to regain ground since. Market commentary has pointed to the detail beneath the headline numbers rather than the quarter itself, with investors fixing on charges linked to the Accelerate Growth restructuring plan, a bigger currency drag than previously expected and higher guided interest expense.

The standout performer was the specialty medicines division, which grew strongly and did most of the heavy lifting. Long-acting HIV therapies Cabenuva and Apretude posted rapid growth, while Nucala benefited from its launch in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Trelegy returned to growth in the United States, although management acknowledged continuing pricing pressure in the American inhaler market.

Research and development spending rose sharply as the company pushed a large number of late-stage studies through the clinic. GSK said it has begun a long list of pivotal trials this year and expects more to start before the year is out, underlining how much of the investment case now rests on pipeline delivery rather than legacy products.

1 Dividend-Paying Biotech Stock to Buy Hand Over Fist in November
sum: - The company’s newest approvals and label expansions should contribute meaningfully to revenue growth.
- Gilead Sciences is attractively valued, and its dividend program appears reliable.

Artificial intelligence (AI) stocks are dominating headlines and attracting much of investors' attention. There is a good reason for that. Some AI companies could produce life-changing returns if infrastructure spending continues to grow. However, there are also attractive investment opportunities elsewhere, particularly for income-seekers, including in the biotech industry. Let's consider one biotech stock long-term dividend investors should seriously consider buying in November: Gilead Sciences (NASDAQ: GILD).

Gilead Sciences has performed well this year. The company's shares are up 39%, while the S&P 500 has climbed a comparatively unimpressive 11%. The biotech leader owes its strong showing in 2026, at least so far, partly to excellent financial results. And the company's third-quarter update added even more fuel to that particular fire.

In the third quarter, Gilead Sciences' revenue increased by 7% year over year to $8.3 billion. Let's remember that Gilead Sciences is still dealing with declining sales of Veklury, a coronavirus medicine. Demand for COVID-19 products -- be it vaccines or therapies -- has decreased substantially in recent years. Gilead Sciences' product sales excluding Veklury grew 16% year over year.

The company continues to lean on its core therapeutic area, HIV, to do most of the heavy lifting. HIV product sales came in at $6.2 billion, up 18% year over year, largely driven by Biktarvy and Descovy for PrEP, the company's most famous HIV drugs. Gilead Sciences' liver disease portfolio also performed well, posting revenue of $927 million, up 13% year over year.

These two segments performed well enough to offset the 18% year-over-year decline in cell therapy sales and the 69% year-over-year decline in Veklury's revenue. On the bottom line, Gilead Sciences posted non-GAAP earnings per share of $2.55, up 3% compared to the year-ago period. Overall, it was a solid quarter for Gilead Sciences, sending the stock higher post-earnings.

FTSE 100 Rises to 10,729.78 as AstraZeneca and BT Offset NatWest's Slump
sum: London's blue-chip index outperformed most global markets on Friday 30 October 2026, with pharmaceutical, telecoms and energy heavyweights cushioning a sharp fall in NatWest and a global technology selloff.

The FTSE 100 closed at 10,729.78 on Friday 30 October 2026, up 7.71 points or 0.07% from Thursday's close of 10,722.07. London's index opened higher and rose about 0.5% in the first hour of trade, according to InstaForex, before giving back most of that advance as the global technology selloff deepened and Wall Street opened sharply lower. The small gain was nonetheless enough to secure the FTSE 100's first monthly rise in three months.

The index's resilience stands out on a day when Japan's Nikkei 225 fell more than 2%, Nasdaq futures dropped more than 2% and Germany's DAX 40 retreated. The FTSE 100's heavy weighting toward pharmaceuticals, energy, consumer staples and mining, and its relatively light exposure to technology, has made it a natural refuge during the latest bout of AI-related selling.

AstraZeneca, one of the three largest companies in the index, was among the leading risers after reporting third-quarter revenue of $16,209 million, up 7% at constant exchange rates, and core earnings per share of $2.79, up 19% at constant exchange rates. The drugmaker reaffirmed its full-year guidance and announced a restructuring programme expected to save around $1.5 billion, which it said would support long-term ambitions including investment in new drug pipelines.

AstraZeneca shares closed about 7% higher, the stock's best day in a year according to Reuters reporting, and GSK added around 2.5%. The broader pharmaceutical sector gained 5.1% over October, its biggest monthly rise since February. Because AstraZeneca carries such a large index weighting, its rally alone more than offset the losses in banks and miners.

NatWest Group was the biggest drag on the index and the worst performer in the STOXX 600, closing nearly 9% lower after its third-quarter net interest income fell short of analyst expectations. The bank reported attributable profit of £1,532 million and operating pre-tax profit of £2.23 billion, up from £2.18 billion a year earlier, with total income of £4.64 billion.

items.t: GSK Shares Sink 7% As Weak Vaccine Demand Rattles Investors Despite Profit Beat
sum: A sharp sell-off in GSK (GSK.L) stock on Wednesday signalled deep investor unease, with shares dropping 7% in morning trading despite the drugs giant beating profit expectations.
The culprit was a disappointing vaccine division, where quarterly revenues slipped 2% to £2.6 billion in the three months ending September 30.

Two of the company’s flagship vaccines drove the decline, with shingles treatment Shingrix posting a 5% drop and RSV shot Arexvy suffering a steeper 24% fall amid weakening demand in the United States.
The retreat in vaccine revenues overshadowed what was otherwise a solid set of numbers for the British pharmaceutical group, which is listed on the FTSE 100.
Core operating profits, stripping out exceptional items and currency movements, climbed 5% to £3.08 billion, comfortably ahead of the £2.93 billion analysts had anticipated.
Pre-tax profits told a different story, however, falling to £1.94 billion in the quarter compared with £2.5 billion during the same period a year earlier.
Bright spots emerged elsewhere in the business, with speciality medicines revenues growing 15% and cancer treatments delivering a 23% jump, helping cushion the vaccine shortfall.

items.t: FTSE 100 Rises to 10,694.50 as Banks Rally on a Lower Than Feared Budget Surcharge While GSK and Housebuilders Slump
sum: London's blue-chip index recovered from early losses on Wednesday, 28 October 2026, closing 7.96 points higher after Chancellor John Healey's first Autumn Budget proved milder for lenders than markets had feared.

The FTSE 100 closed at 10,694.50 points on Wednesday, 28 October 2026, up 7.96 points or 0.07% from Tuesday's close of 10,686.54. The gain was small, but the shape of the session mattered. The index opened lower, traded as low as roughly 10,643 in the morning as GSK and Unilever sold off on results, and only recovered after Chancellor John Healey delivered his first Autumn Budget to Parliament at 12:30 p.m. London time.

The close followed a 0.75% fall on Tuesday, when HSBC and Reckitt Benckiser dragged the index lower on disappointing third-quarter numbers. The mid-cap FTSE 250, which is more exposed to the domestic economy, fell about 0.3%, reversing an earlier rise to a near two-month high.

The headline measure for the stock market was the bank surcharge. Healey raised the corporation tax surcharge on banking profits from 3% to 6% for a temporary 15-month period. Investors had feared a larger increase, with some speculation that the levy would return to its former 8% level, so the announcement triggered relief buying across the sector. RBC Capital Markets analyst Benjamin Toms estimated that the change would be a net headwind of up to 4% for bank profitability in fiscal 2027.

The Budget also included cost-of-living measures, among them scrapping standing charges on gas bills, and the Chancellor said fiscal headroom would narrow to around £15 billion in 2029-30. Market reaction was calm overall, with sterling little changed at about $1.3310 against the US dollar by the London close. Gambling stocks gained after duty changes came in gentler than expected, while housebuilders were hit by a lack of clarity on the timeline and funding of a new first-time buyer scheme.

Banks led the recovery. Lloyds Banking Group closed up 1.7%, Barclays rose 1.6% and NatWest gained 2.0%, according to PA Media, while Standard Chartered added 2.4% after raising its full-year income growth and return targets. StanChart's third-quarter pretax profit jumped 27% to $2.25 billion, beating estimates on strong wealth management and trading income. Gambling operator Entain rose 3.6%.

items.t: FTSE 100 Climbs to 10,724.86, a Three-Week High, as AstraZeneca, GSK and Defence Stocks Lead
sum: London’s blue-chip index closed at its highest level in three weeks on Wednesday, powered by a late rally in pharmaceutical, defence, energy and consumer staples shares, even as hot US inflation data hit Wall Street.

The FTSE 100 closed at 10,724.86 on Wednesday, 14 October 2026, up 74.53 points or 0.70% from Tuesday’s close of 10,650.33. The index opened almost unchanged at 10,649.97, dipped to a session low of 10,641.22 in the first hour of trading and then climbed steadily, hitting an intraday high of 10,731.30 shortly before the close.

London outperformed most major markets on the day. Its heavy weighting towards healthcare, energy, defence and consumer staples, sectors investors tend to favour when inflation and interest rates rise, allowed the index to shrug off a 1.1% fall in the S&P 500 and a 1.9% drop in the Nasdaq Composite.

The official close was 10,724.86, a gain of 0.70% and the index’s highest finish in three weeks. The FTSE 100 now sits about 2.4% below its 52-week high of 10,989.45 and roughly 15.6% above its 52-week low of 9,276.91. Over the past year the index has risen close to 14%.

The intraday path was notable. After a quiet morning, the index briefly fell back towards 10,660 around 13:30 London time, when the US consumer price index was released, before buyers returned. The strongest leg of the rally came in the final hour, taking the index from about 10,690 to above 10,720 by the 16:35 closing auction.

Housebuilder Barratt Redrow was the top performer, rising 4.70%, followed by Burberry, up 3.71%, and AstraZeneca, which gained 3.40%. GSK climbed 3.59%, making pharmaceuticals the biggest contributor to the index’s rise given the two companies’ combined market value. Unilever added 2.5% and British American Tobacco gained 0.8%.

Defence stocks were also in demand as the conflict involving Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia escalated. Babcock International rose about 3.5%, BAE Systems added 2.2% and Rolls-Royce gained 1.2%. In energy, Shell rose 1.2% and BP added 0.7% as Brent crude held near $106 a barrel.

Marston's shares surge as pub firm bets on sports bars
sum: The pub firm said its new Grandstand format, which offers big screens and match-based food and drink offers, has been a standout performer this year
Shares in Marston's surged on Tuesday after the hospitality group announced plans to accelerate the conversion of more than 100 of its pubs into sports bars.
The West Midlands-based pub operator revealed that its new "Grandstand" format, featuring large screens and match-day food and drink promotions, has been its "standout" performer this year.

While the World Cup delivered a significant boost in revenues for Britain's pub operators over the summer, Marston's is banking on sports enthusiasts to sustain its sales well beyond the tournament. Shares in the company climbed nearly 20 per cent to 55p on Tuesday morning.
The group's programme to transform its existing pubs into new formats is "now a proven engine of growth, with Grandstand the standout performer," it told shareholders.
Marston's overhauled 60 of its pubs into new formats last year and plans to refurbish a further 100 next year, with the majority earmarked for the Grandstand concept, as reported by City AM.
These sports bar conversions deliver a 30 per cent uplift in sales on average, the group said, and a return on invested capital of more than 30 per cent.
